title: Let your child play teacher: a bilingual pretend class with three soft toys
description: Line up three soft toys as students and let your child be the teacher. Classroom words and simple instructions in the language you are building, with your child in charge.
book_line: Bilingual English-Spanish vocabulary book for kids: themed word lists and simple activities, read on a Kindle, copied into a notebook when you want them on paper.
pin_title: Let your child play teacher: a bilingual pretend class with three soft toys
body:
Children spend much of their day being told what to do. Giving them the role of teacher flips that, and most children jump at the chance to give the instructions for once.

Set up the classroom: three soft toys in a row on the sofa, a book, a pencil and a piece of paper. You are a student too — the one who gets things slightly wrong.

Before class starts, give your child three teacher instructions in the language you are building. If Spanish: "siéntate" (sit down), "escucha" (listen), "levanta la mano" (raise your hand). If English: "sit down", "listen", "raise your hand" — the English for siéntate, escucha, levanta la mano. Three is enough for a first class. The teacher speaks to one student at a time, which keeps the instructions short.

Then the teacher takes over. Your child tells the toys, and you, what to do. When they tell you to sit down, sit down. When they say "levanta la mano" — or "raise your hand" — raise it, and ask a question when they call on you.

Your questions are where the vocabulary comes in. Hold up the pencil: "¿Qué es esto?" / "what is this?". The teacher answers: "¡un lápiz!" / "a pencil!". Then the book, the paper, the toys themselves. Name something wrong on purpose now and then, and let the teacher correct you.

A few rounds in, let the teacher set a small task: "dibuja un gato" / "draw a cat", or "cuenta hasta cinco" / "count to five". Do the task, show your work, and wait for the verdict.

Keep the class short — ten minutes is a full school day in toy time. End with the teacher saying goodbye: "¡Adiós, clase!" or "goodbye, class!".

If your child is shy about leading at first, be the teacher for one round and then hand the role over. And if they slip into the other language while teaching, answer as the student in the language you are building and keep playing. The game matters more than the language of each sentence.

Next time, add a few classroom words: chair, table, notebook — la silla, la mesa, el cuaderno.
qa_checklist: A bilingual (EN/ES) reader checks both languages, not a tool
No claims about fluency, test scores or developmental outcomes
Every activity works with what is already in the house: no printer, no purchase
Original text written for this page, not lifted from the book
CTA is honest: a Kindle vocabulary book read on a screen, lists copied into a notebook
semantic_review: English body; Spanish singular imperatives (siéntate, escucha, levanta la mano, dibuja, cuenta) addressed to one student at a time, which avoids the regional plural split (siéntense / sentaos). Instructions and questions given in both directions.
claims_check: No outcome promises. The text says what to do and how long it takes; it does not claim fluency, school results or cognitive benefits.

checks_run: direction symmetry (either language may be the target)
resolved: examples run in both directions and the instructions name 'the language you are building'
Spanish kept to short words and phrases with articles and accents checked
closing mention of the book cut to one sentence after the activity is fully explained
instructions kept singular, one student at a time, to avoid the Spain / Latin America plural imperative split
no claim that the role-play increases how much a child speaks
closing sentence about the book removed: the CTA lives on the book card (CLAUDE.md, 12 Sep round four)
